claims.text: The starting Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy is in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing state.
The MA–SPS route consists of ball milling followed by spark plasma sintering.
An optimized MA–SPS thermal profile restrains intermetallic-phase coarsening.
Optimized MA–SPS produces a nanoscale, uniformly dispersed network of fine intermetallic precipitates.
Fine intermetallic precipitates act as nucleation sites for a protective passivating oxide film.
The resulting passivating oxide film is dense, continuous, uniform, and adherent.
MA–SPS processing can yield high corrosion resistance and passivation in Mg-containing multi-principal-element alloys.
The protective film generated by the proposed precipitate mechanism retains superior aqueous corrosion resistance.
The protective film generated by the proposed precipitate mechanism retains superior high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Conventional processing causes excessive growth and clustering of intermetallic compounds.
Coarse or segregated intermetallic compounds interrupt oxide-film continuity or promote oxide-scale spallation.
Optimized MA–SPS samples will contain finer and more uniformly distributed intermetallic phases than conventionally processed controls.
Optimized MA–SPS samples will form a more continuous passivating oxide scale than conventionally processed controls.
Optimized MA–SPS samples will exhibit parabolic high-temperature oxidation behavior.
Optimized MA–SPS samples will have lower corrosion current density and higher corrosion potential than conventionally processed controls.
Conventionally processed samples typically have nonuniform oxide layers and inferior corrosion and oxidation performance.
The proposed performance benefit holds only while processing and service thermal histories remain within an optimized design window.
Exceeding the processing window or service-temperature envelope permits excessive intermetallic growth and negates the passivation benefit.
